# PORTCULLIS training corpus — dataset card

**Status:** Milestone 3. Regenerated by `just data`
([pipeline.py](../packages/training/src/portcullis/training/data/pipeline.py)) — do not hand-edit.
Split statistics and the leakage audit live in
[`docs/benchmarks/leakage-audit.md`](benchmarks/leakage-audit.md), regenerated by the same run.

---

## Composition

| Partition | Rows | Source(s) | Role |
|---|---:|---|---|
| `train` | 16,030 | PromptShield (train) | L2 fine-tuning |
| `validation` | 790 | PromptShield (validation) | calibration, early stopping |
| `test` | 19,937 | PromptShield (test) | headline metrics (TPR @ fixed FPR) |
| `cross_source_eval` | 1,694 | deepset/prompt-injections + jackhhao/jailbreak-classification | transfer eval — sources the model never trained on |
| `hard_negatives_eval` | 70 | authored in-repo | false-positive stress test (the FPR-first thesis, as data) |

All Tier 1 (ADR-0004): ungated, Apache-2.0, redistributable manifests only — no raw corpus is
committed, see `data/processed/corpus.manifest.json` for content hashes. Tier 2 (LMSYS-Chat-1M)
is registered in `sources.py` but was **not fetched** for this run; it requires an authenticated
HF account that has accepted its click-through licence, which this pipeline does not automate.

## Collection methodology

1. **Ingest.** Each Tier-1 source pulled via the HuggingFace `datasets` library, normalised into
   a common `Row` shape (id, text, binary label, source, license, tier). Column names and label
   semantics were verified against a live pull at Milestone 3, not assumed from documentation —
   deepset's label convention (1 = attack) was spot-checked against actual row text.
2. **Near-duplicate clustering.** MinHash/LSH (Broder, 1997 — see `NOTICE`) over word bigrams,
   Jaccard threshold 0.5. Bigrams and this threshold were chosen from measured separation on real
   examples, not guessed: a genuine paraphrase pair scores ~0.6, two prompts sharing only a
   generic attack preamble score ~0.36.
3. **Split.** PromptShield's own train/validation/test skeleton is respected as the backbone.
   Every other Tier-1 source is wholly a held-out evaluation slice (`cross_source_eval`) and
   never contributes a single row to `train`. `hard_negatives_eval` is eval-only by construction.
4. **Leakage remediation.** A near-duplicate cluster spanning two partitions has every member but
   one removed — the train side is always kept; test/validation/cross-source lose to train. This
   is what "disjoint by attack family and source, not by row" (ADR-0004) means at the row level.
5. **Independent audit.** A second, separate check re-derives from the *final* partitions whether
   any cluster still spans more than one — it does not trust the splitter's own bookkeeping.

## Known limitations

- **Binary labels only.** These sources carry injection-vs-benign ground truth, not the 8-class
  attack taxonomy (`direct_override`, `role_play_jailbreak`, ...) L2 is specified to predict.
  Multi-label training data does not exist yet from these sources; Milestone 4 will need to
  either weak-label via the L1 rule taxonomy or find/build a labelled multi-class source. This is
  a real gap, not an oversight — recorded here rather than discovered later.
- **"Family" is source-level, not attack-technique-level**, for the same reason: these corpora do
  not carry fine-grained attack-family annotations to split on. `schema.py`'s `Row.family`
  documents this explicitly.
- **`cross_source_eval` is small** (1,694 rows) relative to `test`. It answers "does this
  generalise to a different source," not "how well," and should not be over-read as a precision
  instrument on its own.
- **PromptShield is heavily templated.** The corpus contains large families of near-identical
  prompts (a "remember this secret key: XXXXXX" wrapper with only the key varying was the single
  largest cluster found, 502+ members). This is exactly what the dedup step exists to catch, but
  it also means the *effective* diversity of `train` is lower than its raw row count suggests.
- **Benign ground truth is PromptShield's definition of "not label 1," not curated production
  traffic.** The original project brief called for real developer-app traffic patterns (support
  bots, coding assistants, RAG Q&A) as an additional benign source. PromptShield's own benign
  rows do cover a range of ordinary instruction-following tasks (grammar correction, summarised
  functions, writing help), which is a reasonable proxy, but a dedicated production-representative
  benign corpus (e.g. Dolly-15k) is future work, not something this run includes.
- **English-dominant.** No deliberate multilingual sourcing at this milestone; a known limitation
  carried over from the threat model.

## A finding worth surfacing on its own

The naive-random-split comparison (`docs/benchmarks/leakage-audit.md`) measured that a plain
80/10/10 row-level split of this pool — ignoring source and near-duplicate structure entirely —
would put a near-duplicate of a training example into **17.4%** of the resulting test set. This
is not a hypothetical argument for why family-disjoint splitting matters; it is the measured cost
of not doing it, on this exact corpus.

A methodological note on how that number was arrived at: the first implementation of the
near-duplicate clusterer had a real bug — single-linkage clustering via union-find let two
completely unrelated prompt templates merge into one cluster through a chain of intermediate
near-neighbours, and the first (uncaught) run of this pipeline reported a naive-leakage figure of
45% on the strength of that bug. It was caught by manually inspecting the largest clusters before
trusting the number, not by any automated check — the fix adds a cohesion validation pass
(`dedup.py`, `_cluster_is_cohesive`) and a regression test that reproduces the exact chain shape
that caused it. The **17.4%** figure above is post-fix.

The fix was verified against the real corpus, not just the synthetic regression test: the five
largest post-fix clusters were sampled (200 random pairs each) and their mean pairwise similarity
checked independently of the cohesion pass that produced them. None showed the chaining
signature (a large fraction of near-orthogonal pairs) — worst case was 26.5% of sampled pairs
below 0.5 similarity with a mean of 0.56, still legitimately cohesive, not a merge artifact.

## Reproducibility caveat

Two consecutive `just data` runs during Milestone 3 produced 38,521 and 38,656 total clusters
respectively — a ~0.35% difference. Row *content* was unaffected (label counts and partition
sizes matched), so this is very likely minor row-ordering variation from HuggingFace's dataset
loader across separate fetches (one run hit a transient network retry), not non-determinism in
the clustering algorithm itself, which is seeded. This is recorded rather than papered over:
exact cluster counts and the manifest's content hash should be treated as accurate to within this
margin across independent reproductions, not as bit-for-bit guaranteed. If this margin needs to
shrink later, pinning each source to an explicit HF dataset revision hash (rather than the
default branch) is the fix.
